title: What financial firms get from a regulatory sandbox
label: 18 November 2026 · Testing financial products with the FCA
summary: A payments company and an AI supplier described different experiences of the Financial Conduct Authority’s sandboxes. Zilch said early discussions with the regulator helped it launch a regulated credit product. Aveni valued the industry exposure but wanted better test data and more sustained discussions about how AI could meet financial rules. They disagreed on how much further guidance firms need, while agreeing that firms remain responsible for protecting customers.

glossary.definition: A programme in which firms develop or test financial products with support or contact from the financial regulator.
The Financial Conduct Authority, which regulates financial services firms in the UK.
Permission to offer consumers credit under the rules governing that activity.
Artificially created information designed to resemble real-world data without revealing actual customers’ details.
AI that can take steps or interact with people to carry out a task, rather than only producing a single response.
UK rules that make named senior staff at financial firms accountable for the areas they oversee.

chapters.title: Two firms, two reasons to join
chapters.takeaway: Zilch sought help with permission to offer regulated credit; Aveni wanted to test AI tools and understand the regulator’s thinking.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What do your companies do, and why did you enter a sandbox?

evidence.quote: Would you please start by telling us a little bit about yourself and the company, and possibly also then indicating why it is you decided to get into a sandbox and what a surprise it was?

turns.speaker: Desmond McNamara
turns.text: Zilch offers payments and credit directly to consumers. We joined in 2019 because we wanted to offer purchases funded by merchants within a regulated credit product. That meant customers could get the protections attached to regulated credit without being charged interest. Talking through our unusual approach with the FCA seemed more useful than simply applying by the usual route. We left with a consumer credit licence roughly nine months to a year later.

evidence.quote: Zilch, which was founded in 2018 and is a direct‑to‑consumer payments and credit business. We entered the regulatory sandbox in April 2019.
Our aim was to show that we could provide merchant-subsidised transactions within a regulated product. We wanted to apply for a consumer credit licence.

We felt that the sandbox programme was a more attractive method for us to engage in a dialogue and have a representative within the innovation area who might be able to provide us some feedback on our application
We exited the sandbox about nine months to a year later with a consumer credit licence.

turns.speaker: Benjamin Cave
turns.text: Aveni builds AI tools for financial firms. We joined a digital sandbox in 2023 while developing an AI language model for UK financial services, then a second programme in 2025 to test checks on AI handling customer conversations. Above all, we wanted direct contact with the FCA about how it was approaching fast-changing technology.

evidence.quote: At Aveni, we are a provider of specialist AI solutions and tools to the financial services industry.

We entered our first sandbox, the digital sandbox, in 2023, as part of our training process for FinLLM, which is the UK’s first large language model specifically aligned to UK financial services regulation. We entered the supercharged sandbox towards the end of 2025 to test our real-time conduct guardrails and approval processes for AI agents handling consumer financial interactions.
Our aim in both cases was to engage directly with the regulator when it comes to these specialist compliance tools

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Did the experience meet your expectations?

evidence.quote: So for both of you it lived up to your expectations.

turns.speaker: Benjamin Cave
turns.text: Partly. The contact and public showcase were useful, but most of the data available was already public. We needed more relevant information for testing and more regular discussions with FCA specialists about how to shape our tools. The programme felt better suited to businesses just starting out.

evidence.quote: From our perspective, it lived up to some of our expectations, such as the regulatory exposure.

It was primarily around access to data, not open-source public data, which is what we largely found inside the sandbox, but specific data developed with industry and the regulator, which could have helped us test those things faster.
We felt like the FCA had a relatively hands-off approach to the programme, which maybe suited earlier-stage businesses that were just setting out on the development of their products

turns.speaker: Desmond McNamara
turns.text: Our experience was very positive. We now lend staff as mentors to other sandbox programmes, giving newer firms commercial feedback as they develop their products.

evidence.quote: We have been very positive about our time in the regulatory sandbox.
We actually provide staff to be mentors to other sandbox programmes from a commercial point of view, so they can have feedback as to how they could learn and develop their products

chapters.title: Customers, test data and guidance
chapters.takeaway: Zilch linked the sandbox to an earlier launch of protected credit, while Aveni said better shared test data could help AI firms avoid developing unsuitable products.

turns.speaker: Lord Sharkey
turns.text: Did taking part improve what customers ultimately received?

evidence.quote: In your view, did participating in the sandbox improve your product or service either directly or indirectly to customers?

turns.speaker: Benjamin Cave
turns.text: It helped indirectly. We test whether AI can deal safely with realistic customers before a firm uses it with the public. The sandbox confirmed that other firms and the FCA saw a need for that work, and it helped lead to live tests with a banking customer. But without the specialist test data we wanted, direct improvements to the product were limited.

evidence.quote: being able to provide safeguards in the form of AI guardrails and testing environments, where financial services institutions can appropriately and adequately test the conduct adherence of those AI solutions against realistic consumers before they expose the consumer to potential harm.
A lot of the businesses—and indeed the FCA—were very, very positive about the need for this approach. It provided us with a lot of confirmation.

Direct improvements to the product were more limited. I would say being unable to access the specialist datasets or regulator‑approved datasets that we were after limited the amount of direct exposure, but it did directly tee up our live tests with one of our banking customers

turns.speaker: Desmond McNamara
turns.text: For our customers, the effect was substantial: we launched a regulated product in 2020. Wider rules for this type of deferred-payment credit took nearly six or seven years to arrive, so our customers could benefit from credit protections much earlier.

evidence.quote: For us, there was definitely a huge impact for consumers, because we were able to launch a consumer product in 2020, which was a regulated product.

The rules on deferred payment credit, which came into existence last year, have taken nearly six or seven years to get to the point where consumers are able to have the benefits of consumer regulation.

turns.speaker: Baroness Bowles of Berkhamsted
turns.text: What kind of data would actually help? And if it’s useful, why limit it to sandbox participants?

evidence.quote: Why could those datasets not be released more generally, so that people who are not in the sandbox could use them as well for testing?
Is there something special about those datasets that you have to keep confidential?

turns.speaker: Benjamin Cave
turns.text: We aren’t asking for companies’ confidential customer records. The FCA and industry could jointly create synthetic data, with the regulator indicating which AI responses are likely to be acceptable. Firms could use it to test their tools before spending time building something the regulator later finds unsuitable. Singapore has developed this kind of shared material.

evidence.quote: For us, it is less about access to a firm’s proprietary data.
being able to provide some level of gold labelling or interpretation of what is and is not acceptable over the top of even synthetic data would be extremely helpful to industry
in Singapore, there has been an active focus there to provide regulator-annotated datasets to all of industry
What that prevents, if that were possible, is providers of all shapes and sizes going off down blind alleys that later prove to be unacceptable to the regulator.

turns.speaker: Lord Hill of Oareford
turns.text: So you’re not saying this useful data is reserved for sandbox members. You’re saying you couldn’t get it there either?

evidence.quote: it is not that you are getting the data you want only in the sandbox; it is that you are not getting the data you want in the sandbox.

turns.speaker: Benjamin Cave
turns.text: That’s correct.

evidence.quote: That is correct.

turns.speaker: Desmond McNamara
turns.text: There’s another side to the data question. UK credit firms already supply information to credit bureaus, which sell access to it. Firms can buy data for developing products; the FCA isn’t their only possible source. We didn’t use the digital sandbox ourselves.

evidence.quote: All the firms in the UK provide all their credit data to bureaus, and that is an entire business model where bureaus then sell that data back to firms, making that data visible and accessible for firms to go and buy and connect to today.
We do not have a particular use case, because we have not used that digital sandbox, but the FCA is not the sole provider of data that is needed to be able to develop business cases.

turns.speaker: Lord Eatwell
turns.text: The FCA also gets to learn what firms are developing. Can you tell whether its approach changed as a result?

evidence.quote: some of the key beneficiaries in all this are the regulators, because they are learning what is going on
did it change anything?

turns.speaker: Benjamin Cave
turns.text: It’s hard to tell. We contributed to recent FCA guidance on good AI practice, but can’t establish whether the sandbox itself affected it. It’s right for the FCA to learn from firms. We’d also benefit from ongoing discussions with its experts; otherwise a firm might spend a year or two building in the wrong direction.

evidence.quote: As a participant in the sandbox it is hard to establish whether the regulator’s approach changed. We have certainly fed into the AI good practice guidance, which was published last month.
Whether that directly connected to the sandbox, though, as opposed to the call for expressions of interest, is hard to ascertain from the outside.
The regulator is a key beneficiary, and that is as it should be.
If that needs to wait for a live testing environment, that is sometimes a year or two of development in potentially the wrong direction.

turns.speaker: Desmond McNamara
turns.text: We benefited too. When later credit rules were discussed, officials could look at the digital lending process we’d built. But firms also need to maintain contact after a sandbox ends. We’ve kept a broader relationship with the FCA, and I hope it helps the regulator as well.

evidence.quote: the process and journeys that we had built were used as quite a good example of how digital lending could be done in a regulated format.
It is also a responsibility on firms to have ongoing relationships and to build upon those.
It has benefited us as a firm and I hope it has also benefited the FCA in thinking about how to deliver innovative products in new ways.

chapters.title: Who is responsible when AI goes wrong?
chapters.takeaway: Both witnesses favoured responsibility for firms rather than rigid new AI rules, but differed over whether existing guidance gives firms enough confidence.

turns.speaker: Lord Lilley
turns.text: As agentic AI takes on more tasks, is the FCA trying to work out which rules cover it and how to treat it differently from a human?

evidence.quote: we came across the issue of AI as it is, and agentic AI as it is becoming.
Is that what the FCA is trying to work out in its work with you, where the regulatory perimeter should be and how it should treat agentic AI as against humans?

turns.speaker: Benjamin Cave
turns.text: That’s part of it. The FCA’s position is that the humans responsible for an AI system remain accountable under the senior managers regime. The difficult question is how those people can know that a fast-changing system is still following the rules. Industry needs to solve that problem, and we’re seeking more clarity from the regulator.

evidence.quote: That is certainly part of what the FCA is grappling with
Whatever your AI solutions are, they devolve to the responsibility of the humans who are responsible for them

how you could ever satisfy a human that a very fast-moving AI system is remaining in alignment or inside of its regulatory perimeter. That remains a problem that needs to be solved by the industry and we continue to seek more engagement with the regulator

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What more should the FCA do about agentic AI?

evidence.quote: what more should the sandbox do, or the FCA do, to wrestle the problem of agentic AI and come up with a satisfactory regulatory framework?

turns.speaker: Benjamin Cave
turns.text: Keeping the focus on what happens to customers, rather than prescribing every technical step, is right. But firms still wonder what evidence the FCA would expect if an AI system harmed someone. We’ve seen many trials and few full launches, including among large firms we work with. Risk staff are understandably nervous about how the FCA would judge them if something went wrong. Earlier, sustained discussions could help.

evidence.quote: a focus on the outcome for the consumer is the right one to maintain.

If there is an incident or a redress, will the FCA look unfavourably on the senior manager for not having sought more deeply for assurances on these things, or will it consider the assurances that it was provided with sufficient?

We have seen an awful lot of firms pilot the use of agentic AI directed to the consumer or behind the scenes. We have seen very few of those firms, including larger financial services institutions that we work with, make their way to production.
a nervousness or an understandable risk from the second line and from those chief risk officers about how they will be viewed by the FCA if something did go wrong.

turns.speaker: Desmond McNamara
turns.text: As a chief risk officer, I think the rules are already sufficient. Detailed rules for products that haven’t even been built could restrict innovation. Firms should check their models, remain responsible for good customer outcomes and share lessons across the industry. We don’t need a new rule for every possible use of AI.

evidence.quote: I am the chief risk officer for the firm, and I feel that the rules are more than sufficient already. Too-prescriptive rules will limit innovation. The outcomes-based approach is the right approach.
There is always a benefit of having some thematic learnings that will then get shared back across the industry on a regular basis
there are lots of rules on model governance today that are already in place.

turns.speaker: Benjamin Cave
turns.text: I agree we aren’t asking for more detailed rules. We’re asking the FCA to talk through how it would view responsibility when harm occurs, including whether that harm could reasonably have been foreseen.

evidence.quote: I totally agree with you; it is not that more prescriptive rules are required, but it is a general nervousness about the way that those things will be treated.
Is the harm foreseeable, or is the harm not foreseeable?
We are certainly not asking for more prescriptive rules, but more engagement with the regulator and more clarification of its thinking on these issues

turns.speaker: Lord Griffiths of Fforestfach
turns.text: If technology is changing this quickly, does the FCA need more specialist people to keep up with firms?

evidence.quote: if the FCA wants to engage with you more in an area that is changing at a tremendous pace, it needs to hire people with more skills in the business, who will be, by definition, more expensive. Is that the ultimate logic of where you are going?

turns.speaker: Benjamin Cave
turns.text: The people who understand financial rules often aren’t the people building AI models, and vice versa. Firms can develop a working tool and only later ask how to control its risks to customers. That’s harder than considering those risks from the start. Regular discussions between the FCA and industry about difficult examples would help both sides.

evidence.quote: Those who are experts in the regulation are rarely the people building and maintaining the models. Those who are experts in the models are rarely the experts in the interpretation or enforcement of the compliance and regulation.

agents and AI solutions are developed functionally, with very little reference to regulatory oversight, model risk governance or foreseeable consumer harms, and then they are subjected to those at a later stage.
The FCA’s sustained engagement with that over repeated working groups, as opposed to individually or at a point in time through a showcase, would be of great benefit.

turns.speaker: Desmond McNamara
turns.text: There are practical benefits to consider. If someone needs help from a financial firm late at night, a well-controlled AI assistant might give a good answer instead of making them wait until morning. Our job is to put those controls in place and check that customers get good outcomes; that responsibility doesn’t transfer to the FCA.

evidence.quote: If a customer has a question at 9 pm, or is maybe feeling very vulnerable at 10 pm or 11 pm, and they want to get an answer, surely it would be better to give them a very good answer using an AI agent that has certain controls and limitations than ask them to call back at 9 am the following day.
My responsibility today as a chief risk officer is to ensure we have the controls in place to do that.
As firms, it is our responsibility to deliver good outcomes to consumers. It is not the FCA’s responsibility.

turns.speaker: Benjamin Cave
turns.text: But a model’s behaviour can change very quickly. An answer that’s safe at 9 am might cause harm at 10 am. Firms need to monitor it continuously, and the FCA will have to consider what evidence a senior manager needs to be confident that it remains safe.

evidence.quote: models can drift hour to hour. A model that gives a perfectly good answer to a consumer at 9 am might be unwittingly engendering harm for that consumer at 10 am.

How you monitor those things in real time and what level of evidence and satisfaction a senior manager needs to properly feel accountable for the ongoing performance of that model is something that the regulator will have to wrestle with.

chapters.title: Different programmes for different firms
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses saw value in several routes to FCA contact, but disagreed about grouping similar firms and how much support a supplier needs.

turns.speaker: Lord Lilley
turns.text: Would firms benefit from joining a sandbox alongside others working on similar problems, or would competitors be reluctant to share ideas?

evidence.quote: perhaps half a dozen different firms would come into a sandbox with similar or related products that they are developing. It might be useful for them to exchange ideas, but it might also be difficult, I would have thought, if they are competitors.

turns.speaker: Desmond McNamara
turns.text: Mentors can help with that: firms can ask people who’ve already been through a programme, rather than current competitors. It might help to have mentors from a wider range of firms. But when Zilch joined, I’d rather have got on with our application than waited six months or a year for enough similar companies to form a group.

evidence.quote: It was almost easier for them to come and ask someone who had been through a programme, rather than maybe someone who was currently in their programme.
if there were more mentors from a broader range of firms, that might be helpful
I would much rather have got on with it and gone through, rather than wait for six months or a year until there were enough people to discuss the element.

turns.speaker: Benjamin Cave
turns.text: For us, a group facing the same problem and at a similar stage of development would have been useful. Many participants were only beginning to build products; the free computing resources and available data meant more to them than to us. A better-matched group could also attract mentors and FCA specialists with the right experience. Suppliers like us and firms selling directly to consumers need different kinds of support.

evidence.quote: we would most certainly have found it helpful had there been a theme and a cohort of businesses that were alike in two ways. Number one, they were grappling with the same issue, but, number two, they were of roughly the same stage in their maturity and development.
many of the firms were pre product. They were extremely nascent.
Grouping things in cohorts with a more common theme and a more common stage would allow you to centralise and concentrate the types of mentors that are available.

they benefit from different constructs in their sandboxes. Those journeys look rather different for those who are trying to gauge the FCA’s posture on something so that they can supply the industry, and those who are themselves suppliers of solutions to the end consumer.

turns.speaker: Lord Davies of Brixton
turns.text: Do sandboxes actually cause more innovation, or mainly help firms develop ideas they would have pursued anyway? There’s innovation in countries without them.

evidence.quote: I have seen all the evidence that shows that they facilitate innovation. What I am not so clear on is that they actually promote innovation.
We have a counterfactual in the States, where they do not have sandboxes and we are told there is a lot of innovation going on there.

turns.speaker: Benjamin Cave
turns.text: Firms will innovate anyway. As a supplier, we approach the regulator to learn whether what we’re building seems consistent with its rules—not to get an FCA endorsement. We’d benefit from a way to show the FCA more of our work and discuss concerns over time. That’s what I think many firms in our sandbox wanted but didn’t quite receive.

evidence.quote: Firms are innovating anyway. Firms will get on with innovation.
We cannot get an FCA endorsement, and, to be very clear, we would not want one. We understand that the regulator must be assiduously neutral here.
having a pathway, whether that is a sandbox, sustained working group engagement or some other construct, for a firm to be able to show the FCA more of what it is working on
From our experience, that is what most of the firms in the supercharged sandbox were after, and what none of us quite received from our participation.

turns.speaker: Desmond McNamara
turns.text: It’s firms’ job to invent products, not the FCA’s. The FCA can offer several ways to get help with different needs, such as permission to offer a service, data or technology testing. That variety suits us better than one process for everyone. We’ve been able to innovate here.

evidence.quote: It is difficult for the FCA to create innovation. It is for firms to create and be innovative.
These multiple pathways, while complex to understand, create different opportunities for firms to go down. The idea that one size fits all is not what we want.
We certainly feel that we can innovate our products here; that is why we are here.

If you need a licence, you need data, you need to test some technology or you want to look into, as a previous speaker had, crypto and tokenisation, those are all areas where firms can approach the FCA and engage in some way, shape or form

turns.speaker: Lord Hill of Oareford
turns.text: How can the FCA give you useful direction on AI if its staff may know less about new technology than you do?

evidence.quote: Are you not always going to know more about developments in AI than the regulator possibly can? How does that work? How can the regulator keep up?

turns.speaker: Benjamin Cave
turns.text: I’m not asking the FCA to predict new laws; that isn’t solely its decision. I’m asking for regular discussions with several providers about how existing rules might apply as AI develops. We could explain what’s changing, and FCA specialists could point out possible concerns about customer harm or who’s accountable. Both sides would learn.

evidence.quote: In terms of changes to the regulation, I fully accept that. That lies outside the FCA’s gift
ongoing working groups between the FCA and multiple providers, not just a single provider

On our side as providers, it would provide us with an understanding of how the FCA regulatory experts, for what of a better word, respond to those. Do they raise concerns about how that would be interpreted within the senior managers regime? Do they raise concerns about specific kinds of foreseeable harm that need to be controlled for? That lets both sides learn from each other in an ongoing relationship.

chapters.title: Cost, openness and what to change
chapters.takeaway: Neither witness described high direct participation costs, but Aveni warned that public showcases and short-term programmes can’t replace sustained regulatory discussion.

turns.speaker: Lord Vaux of Harrowden
turns.text: What did joining and taking part cost you, compared with other routes?

evidence.quote: How much did it cost to get into it in the first place? What was the cost of being in there? How might those costs compare with alternative ways of getting to the same thing

turns.speaker: Benjamin Cave
turns.text: Our direct costs were small: mainly staff time we could otherwise have spent with customers or developing products. Applying and taking part were straightforward. The final showcase was well run and helped put us in front of other firms.

evidence.quote: Our costs are fairly minimal. As you would expect from a provider, we already had the technology, so our costs were really just the people and engagement cost, and the opportunity cost, I suppose, of dedicating those resources to engagement with the FCA, as opposed to with our clients or on innovation of our products.

The FCA did a good job of setting up a streamlined application process. We found it very straightforward to participate in the sessions. The showcase was slick and well organised at the end, and gave us good exposure to industry.

turns.speaker: Desmond McNamara
turns.text: I’m not aware of a separate charge for applying or taking part. Our staff spent time on it, but that was time well spent: explaining an unusual product to the FCA mattered to us. For a more conventional change, we later used the normal application route.

evidence.quote: I am not aware of there being any specific costs allocated to a firm for applying to or being in any of the sandbox programmes.
we feel it was time and money well spent, because it allowed us to explain our product and services versus the more traditional route.
We have separately used the traditional route, where we had a more traditional product change that we wanted to do and therefore did not need to have that additional engagement.

turns.speaker: Baroness Donaghy
turns.text: Is “sandbox” still a helpful name, or would a clearer description of testing, mentoring and contact with the FCA help newer firms understand what’s offered?

evidence.quote: whether phrases such as “engagement”, “multiple methods to test a product”, “mentoring”, would be more useful, first for the outside world to understand, and secondly for newer firms coming in to understand precisely what the process is.
Are you quite happy to keep using the word “sandbox” even though it does not mean anything any more?

turns.speaker: Benjamin Cave
turns.text: I’m not keen on the name. It can make serious work sound like playing around. More importantly, I’d like programmes where the FCA works with firms on a problem over time, rather than admitting them, largely leaving them alone, then holding a showcase. The FCA’s separate live testing programme offers the kind of sustained feedback I mean.

evidence.quote: I am not a lover of the word “sandbox”
It creates a slightly infantile impression of playing around with something.
you set them up, you announce them, they have grand PR, firms join, they are left largely alone, and then you close them down with a showcase.
the live testing regime. Providers enter with serious consumer‑facing AI solutions and get sustained engagement from the regulator and sustained feedback

turns.speaker: Desmond McNamara
turns.text: I’m less worried about the name than whether the different forms of support work. New approaches, such as extra help for growing firms, can be tried and stopped if they prove unnecessary. I accept, though, that the names may make it harder for people outside the system to see what’s available.

evidence.quote: I am less concerned about the naming of them.

The scale-up unit and suchlike are a response from the industry, saying there may be a need to help firms a little bit more in that scale-up phase. Do we know exactly what it is yet? The answer is no, so there is a first test cohort of this. It may turn out to be a terrible idea and not to be needed, in which case it should end.
I agree the naming probably makes it complex for those who are not directly in there and maybe prevents some people getting involved

turns.speaker: Lord Smith of Kelvin
turns.text: If firms present their work at the end, could competitors learn enough to copy them?

evidence.quote: when they come out of the sandbox, do they publish all the full details of that product so that you can compete directly as a non-participant?

turns.speaker: Benjamin Cave
turns.text: That worry is real for some participants, especially when large firms attend. We shared our test results, not most of the valuable details of how our technology works. I didn’t find the programme anti-competitive for us, and the showcases are a good way to meet industry—but firms have reason to choose carefully what they reveal.

evidence.quote: The presence of larger institutions looking in on their innovations and their work and then, as you put it earlier, transposing that work to their own context does provide a threat. It does provide an incentive not to showcase all your IP in these environments
we did not publish most of our IP that we walked into the sandbox with as a result of the sandbox there. We published a lot of the testing results of that.
I did not feel it was anti-competitive for us to get together
They are an excellent industry platform.

turns.speaker: Desmond McNamara
turns.text: At the showcases I’ve attended, firms decide how much to present. If they’re trying to sell a service, meeting potential partners there can be useful. We don’t build every part of our business ourselves, and we might find a company whose product fits what we need.

evidence.quote: Those are generally quite open forum invites where anyone can attend. It is up to those firms to decide how much they want to say
We do not build our entire architecture end to end. We work with lots of partners, so we might bump into a new partner at one of those events
